notes: Ahasuerus is the Hebrew form of the king’s name. Cush is the region south of Egypt; “Ethiopia” in older usage should not be equated exactly with the modern country.
Several material names are rare or uncertain. The paving terms are rendered with conventional possibilities; their precise mineral identifications cannot be established from this verse alone.
The command specifies Vashti’s royal crown. It does not say that she was to appear naked.
The final language clause is difficult: it may concern the household’s language or the language in which male authority was to be announced. The draft keeps the direct wording.
vocabulary: Citadel
A fortified royal or administrative center, distinguished here from the wider city.
Eunuch
A male court attendant; the term commonly refers to a castrated man, though it can also function as a court title.

sections.12: The women’s turns before the king

notes: “Who had been taken into exile” can be connected with Mordecai or an ancestor in the preceding genealogy, especially Kish. The Hebrew does not remove this ambiguity.
Hadassah is Esther’s other name. She is Mordecai’s cousin, whom he raises as a daughter.
Esther is “taken” into the palace. The account does not describe a voluntary modern beauty contest.
The provincial benefit may be a holiday or some form of remission or relief; its exact administrative meaning is uncertain.
The text mentions a second gathering of virgins without explaining its relationship to the earlier gathering.
The Hebrew describes being hung on wood. The wording can include hanging or impalement; “wooden stakes” does not establish the exact execution method.
vocabulary: Concubines
Women in a recognized sexual relationship with a man whose status was below that of a full wife. Here they remain in guarded royal quarters.
Chronicles
An official written record of events. This particular entry returns to the story in chapter 6.

sections.7: A decree to destroy the Jews

notes: “Agagite” evokes Agag, the Amalekite king in 1 Samuel 15. The label is retained without adding an unexpressed genealogy.
The narrative says Mordecai is a Jew but does not explicitly explain why he refuses the gestures. A specific claim about idolatry is not added.
The Hebrew names Adar as the resulting month; the thirteenth day is stated in verse 13.
The grant of the silver can be understood as waiving Haman’s payment or allowing him control of the funds. The direct wording leaves the issue open.
vocabulary: Pur
A lot used to select a date. The Hebrew immediately explains the foreign term; it will give its name to Purim.
Talent
A large unit of weight. Ten thousand talents describes an enormous amount of silver.
Signet ring
A seal used to authorize documents in the king’s name.

notes: The Hebrew switches to a plural subject, “they,” after naming Hathach earlier. The switch is retained.
Mordecai speaks of relief from “another place” and asks “who knows?” The Hebrew does not explicitly name God or turn the question into certainty.
Fasting is stated, but prayer is not expressly mentioned in this Hebrew passage. The repetition “if I perish, I perish” retains Esther’s acknowledgment of danger.
vocabulary: Sackcloth and ashes
Visible signs of grief and distress.
Scepter
A royal staff. The king’s extension of it grants an exception to the stated death penalty.

notes: “Half the kingdom” is the king’s extravagant offer of generosity; the narrative does not describe a formal division of the realm.
Esther delays stating her full request. The narrator does not explain her motive for the second banquet.
Fifty cubits is an exceptionally tall structure, roughly 22–25 meters depending on the cubit used. The exact structure and execution method remain uncertain.
vocabulary: Cubit
A length based on the forearm. The ancient measurement is retained in the text.

sections.1: The forgotten service is read aloud

notes: The king’s sleeplessness is stated without an explicit cause. No divine explanation is inserted into the Hebrew narrative.
Bigthana is the form here of the name Bigthan in 2:21.
The crown most naturally attaches to the horse, the nearest antecedent, though the wording has also been understood with reference to the king.
The prediction of Haman’s fall belongs to his advisors’ speech. Its repeated falling language is retained.
vocabulary: Delights to honor
A repeated phrase linking Haman’s imagined reward to Mordecai’s actual public honor.
Head covered
A visible expression of grief or shame in this scene.
